citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The anterior surface of the coccyx can be palpated with the gloved finger in the anal canal.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: Which specific ligament helps form the boundaries of the greater and lesser sciatic foramina, which are essential passages near the pelvic joints?
options: The round ligament of the uterus
The suspensory ligament of the ovary
correctOption: The sacrotuberous ligament
optionExplanations: The median umbilical ligament is the remnant of the urachus and connects the bladder apex to the umbilicus.
The puboprostatic ligaments are thickenings of pelvic fascia that stabilize the bladder neck and prostate to the pubic bones.
The round ligament of the uterus maintains the anteversion of the uterus and passes through the inguinal canal.
The sacrotuberous ligament, along with the sacrospinous ligament, converts the sciatic notches of the hip bone into the greater and lesser sciatic foramina.
The suspensory ligament of the ovary contains the ovarian vessels and nerves as they cross the pelvic inlet.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments help form the greater and lesser sciatic foramina, which are parts of the pelvic outlet.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: Which obstetric landmark represents the upper posterior margin of the pelvic inlet and serves as the primary site for the lumbosacral articulation?
correctOption: Sacral promontory
optionExplanations: The sacral hiatus is the inferior opening of the sacral canal used for caudal anesthesia, located far distal to the lumbosacral joint.
The ischial spine is a landmark for the pudendal nerve block and defines the pelvic outlet/sciatic notches, not the inlet.
The pubic crest is the anterior margin of the pelvic inlet, not the posterior articulating site.
The iliac crest is a superior boundary of the false pelvis, not the articulating site for L5/S1.
The sacral promontory is the anterior-superior edge of the S1 vertebral body and articulates with L5 via the intervertebral disc.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The sacral promontory is the upper posterior margin of the pelvic inlet and is an important obstetric landmark used when measuring the size of the pelvis.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: In the male, what is the anatomical relationship between the terminal portion of the vas deferens and the urinary bladder, relative to the pelvic floor?
options: It is posterior to the sacrum
It lies side by side on the base of the bladder
It lies on the superior surface of the bladder
It is lateral to the sacroiliac joint
correctOption: It lies side by side on the base of the bladder
optionExplanations: The sacrum is the posterior wall of the pelvis; the vas deferens is anterior to the rectum, which is in turn anterior to the sacrum.
The vasa deferentia descend on the posterior surface (base) of the bladder, medially to the seminal vesicles, before joining the ducts of the vesicles.
The vas deferens does not pierce bone; it passes through the inguinal canal and over the pelvic brim.
The superior surface of the bladder is covered by peritoneum and related to the sigmoid colon/ileum, not the vasa deferentia.
The vasa deferentia are medial structures once they reach the bladder base, not lateral to the SI joint.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The two vasa deferentia lie side by side on the base of the bladder and separate the seminal vesicles from each other (see Fig. 9.13).

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: A patient experiences pain that radiates from the lower back down the leg following the distribution of the sciatic nerve. During the examination, the clinician notes the relationship between the nerve roots and the sacral canal. Where does the subarachnoid space typically terminate in relation to the sacrum?
options: At the tip of the coccyx
At the level of the first sacral vertebra
At the level of the sacral hiatus
At the level of the second sacral spine
correctOption: At the level of the second sacral spine
optionExplanations: The tip of the coccyx is the terminal bony point of the pelvis and does not contain meningeal spaces.
The S1 level is too superior for the termination of the subarachnoid space in adults.
The sacral hiatus is where the extradural space (not subarachnoid) terminates, approximately 2 inches above the coccyx.
The subarachnoid space ends at the level of the second sacral vertebra (S2), which is clinically marked by the level of the PSIS dimples and the middle of the sacro-iliac joint.
The sacrococcygeal joint is the terminal articulation of the spine and is distal to the subarachnoid space limit.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": It lies at the bottom of a small skin dimple and on a level with the second sacral spine, which coincides with the lower limit of the subarachnoid space.

coreConcept: Articular Components of the Sacroiliac Joint
statement: What are the specific articular surfaces involved in the formation of the sacro-iliac joint?
options: The auricular surfaces of the sacrum and the ilium.
The sacral promontory and the body of L5.
The ischial spine and the coccygeal base.
The pubic crest and the pectineal line.
The head of the femur and the acetabulum.
correctOption: The auricular surfaces of the sacrum and the ilium.
optionExplanations: The sacro-iliac joint is formed by the articulation of the ear-shaped (auricular) surfaces on the lateral aspects of the sacrum and the medial aspects of the ilium.
The sacral promontory and the body of L5 form the symphyseal part of the lumbosacral joint.
The ischial spine is a landmark for the pudendal nerve; it does not articulate with the coccygeal base (which forms the sacrococcygeal joint with the sacral apex).
The pubic crest and pectineal line are features of the pelvic brim and do not form a joint articulation.
The head of the femur and acetabulum form the hip joint (a ball-and-socket synovial joint).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The common iliac artery ends at the pelvic inlet in front of the sacroiliac joint...

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: Which specific anatomic classification correctly describes the articulation found in the midline between the bodies of the pubic bones?
correctOption: Secondary cartilaginous joint
optionExplanations: Synovial plane joints involve a joint cavity and allow gliding; the pubic symphysis lacks a synovial cavity and is cartilaginous.
Primary cartilaginous joints (synchondroses) are united by hyaline cartilage and typically involve growth plates, which is not the case for the adult pubic symphysis.
A fibrous syndesmosis is joined by interosseous ligaments (like the tibiofibular joint). While ligaments support the symphysis, the primary union is fibrocartilage.
A synovial pivot joint allows rotation around a longitudinal axis (like the atlantoaxial joint), which is anatomically distinct from the pubic symphysis structure.

The pubic symphysis is a secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis) where the bone ends are covered by hyaline cartilage and united by a strong disc of fibrocartilage, designed for weight-bearing and limited movement.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The symphysis pubis (see Figs. 8.1 and 8.22) lies in the midline between the bodies of the pubic bones and can be palpated as a solid structure through the fat that is present in this region.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: The sacral hiatus, a critical site for caudal anesthesia, is located at which distance relative to the tip of the coccyx?
options: About 2 in. (5 cm) above the tip of the coccyx
Directly posterior to the lumbosacral joint
Level with the second sacral spine
At the level of the pubic tubercle
correctOption: About 2 in. (5 cm) above the tip of the coccyx
optionExplanations: The sacral hiatus is the inferior opening of the sacral canal, located approximately 5 cm superior to the coccygeal tip.
The lumbosacral joint is at the top of the sacrum; the hiatus is at the bottom.
The tip of the coccyx itself is 1 inch behind the anus, not the hiatus.
The second sacral spine level marks the end of the subarachnoid space and the middle of the SI joint, not the hiatus.
The pubic tubercle is an anterior landmark; the sacral hiatus is posterior.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The hiatus lies about 2 in. (5 cm) above the tip of the coccyx and beneath the skin of the cleft between the buttocks.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
coreConcept: Anatomical Composition of the Bony Pelvis
statement: Which of the following structures constitutes the complete bony pelvis as defined by its skeletal articulations?
options: The lumbar vertebrae and the ossa coxae
The paired hip bones and the sacrum only
The paired hip bones, the sacrum, and the coccyx
The sacrum and the fifth lumbar vertebra
The ilium, ischium, pubis, and sacrum
correctOption: The paired hip bones, the sacrum, and the coccyx
optionExplanations: The lumbar vertebrae are part of the posterior abdominal wall and the axial skeleton but are not considered part of the 'bony pelvis' itself.
This option is incorrect as it omits the coccyx, which is an integral part of the bony pelvic ring and its articulations.
Correct. The bony pelvis is a complete skeletal unit formed by the two hip bones (which are each composed of the fused ilium, ischium, and pubis) and the midline sacrum and coccyx.
This refers to the lumbosacral junction, which is only one part of the pelvic articulations and not the entire bony pelvis.
This option lists the embryonic components of the hip bone separately but omits the coccyx and the paired nature of the hip bones.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The bony pelvis consists of the paired hip bones (os coxae), the sacrum, and the coccyx.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: Which vascular structure's position relative to the sacroiliac joint must be accounted for when performing a posterior pelvic dissection?
options: The deep dorsal vein of the penis
correctOption: The internal iliac vein
optionExplanations: The testicular artery enters the inguinal canal and does not enter the true pelvis or cross the sacroiliac joint.
The internal iliac vein is a major systemic vessel that ascends directly anterior to the sacroiliac joint; trauma to this area can cause significant hemorrhage.
The deep dorsal vein of the penis passes under the symphysis pubis, an anterior structure, not the posterior sacroiliac joint.
The inferior mesenteric vein is located higher in the abdomen/pelvis and is a tributary of the portal system, not directly related to the SI joint surface.
The superior vesical artery is a distal branch of the internal iliac artery that supplies the bladder; it is not the primary vessel marking the SI joint level.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The internal iliac vein... passes upward in front of the sacroiliac joint and joins the external iliac vein to form the common iliac vein.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
coreConcept: Mechanical Stabilization of the Lumbosacral Joint
statement: The lumbosacral joint is reinforced by the iliolumbar ligaments. Which step in the mechanical stabilization of the pelvis do these ligaments perform to prevent the L5 vertebra from sliding anteriorly on the sacral promontory?
options: Connecting the coccygeal cornua to the sacral hiatus
Promoting the posterior rotation of the sacrum around the vertical axis
Facilitating the widening of the pelvic inlet during the first stage of labor
Inhibiting the descent of the sacral promontory into the lesser pelvis
Limiting the anterior glide of L5 on S1 by anchoring the transverse processes to the iliac crest
correctOption: Limiting the anterior glide of L5 on S1 by anchoring the transverse processes to the iliac crest
optionExplanations: This describes the sacrococcygeal ligaments, which are distinct from the lumbosacral supports.
Posterior rotation of the sacrum is counternutation; the iliolumbar ligaments focus on the L5-S1 junction rather than primary sacral rotation.
Widening of the inlet is a hormonal/mechanical process during labor; the iliolumbar ligaments are generally restrictive/stabilizing rather than facilitatory for labor widening.
The sacral promontory's position is inherently part of the sacrum; the ligaments stabilize the vertebra relative to it rather than 'inhibiting the descent' of the promontory itself.

The lumbosacral joint (L5-S1) is prone to anterior sliding (spondylolisthesis) due to the tilt of the sacral promontory. The iliolumbar ligaments provide critical mechanical stabilization by anchoring the L5 transverse processes to the iliac crests, preventing this anterior glide.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The sacral promontory is the upper posterior margin of the pelvic inlet and is an important obstetric landmark used when measuring the size of the pelvis.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
coreConcept: Developmental Anatomy of the Hip Bone
statement: What is the structural composition of the immature hip bone before fusion occurs during puberty, impacting the mechanics of the pelvic girdle?
options: An articulation between the femur and the sacrum only
A single ossified mass centered at the obturator foramen
Separate ilium, ischium, and pubis joined by triradiate cartilage
Two lateral halves joined by the median sacral crest
A cartilaginous sheath covering the entire pelvic brim
correctOption: Separate ilium, ischium, and pubis joined by triradiate cartilage
optionExplanations: The femur articulates with the hip bone (acetabulum), and the hip bone articulates with the sacrum; there is no direct femur-sacrum articulation.
The hip bone develops from three distinct primary centers of ossification, not a single mass.
In children, the hip bone is not yet a single bone; the three components (ilium, ischium, and pubis) meet at the acetabulum in a Y-shaped (triradiate) cartilage which ossifies after puberty.
The median sacral crest is the fused spinous processes of the sacrum, not a junction for the hip bones.
The pelvic brim is a bony landmark; while it has cartilaginous precursors, the 'immature hip bone' refers specifically to the three-part division at the acetabulum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The immature hip bone consists of the separate ilium, ischium, and pubis. These join by way of the triradiate cartilage in the acetabulum.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
coreConcept: Midline Components of the Posterior Abdominal Wall
statement: A trauma patient has a suspected fracture of the posterior abdominal wall. The physician reviews the midline structures to check for lumbosacral integrity. According to the anatomical composition of the posterior abdominal wall, which structures form its midline portion?
options: The external oblique and transversus abdominis aponeuroses
The 12th ribs and the iliacus muscles
The five lumbar vertebrae and their intervertebral discs
The psoas muscles and the quadratus lumborum
The triradial cartilage and the acetabulum
correctOption: The five lumbar vertebrae and their intervertebral discs
optionExplanations: These are components of the anterior and lateral abdominal walls, not the posterior wall.
Ribs and iliacus muscles are lateral components of the posterior wall, not midline.
Correct. The lumbosacral region begins with the lumbar vertebrae and discs which constitute the midline of the posterior wall.
Psoas and quadratus lumborum are muscular components located lateral to the vertebral column.
The triradial cartilage is the fusion point within the acetabulum of the hip bone, located laterally in the pelvis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The posterior abdominal wall is formed in the midline by the five lumbar vertebrae and their intervertebral discs

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: When contrasting the surface anatomy dimples of the posterior pelvis, the level of the posterior superior iliac spine is a critical landmark for which underlying structural relation?
options: The level of the third sacral vertebra
The apex of the bladder in its empty state
The junction of the descending colon and sigmoid colon
The middle of the sacroiliac joint
The bifurcation of the aorta into common iliac arteries
correctOption: The middle of the sacroiliac joint
optionExplanations: The level of the second sacral spine (S2) coincides with the PSIS, not the third sacral vertebra (S3), which marks the start of the rectum.
The apex of the empty bladder lies behind the upper margin of the symphysis pubis, which is an anterior structure.
The descending colon becomes the sigmoid colon at the pelvic brim, but the PSIS is specifically used to mark the sacroiliac joint depth.
The posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) lies at the bottom of a skin dimple and marks the level of S2 and the middle of the sacroiliac joint.
The bifurcation of the aorta occurs at the level of the fourth lumbar vertebra, significantly superior to the posterior superior iliac spine.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": It also coincides with the level of the middle of the sacroiliac joint.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: Which of the following describes the anatomical plane in which the pubic symphysis lies within the pelvic girdle?
correctOption: Median sagittal plane
optionExplanations: The horizontal plane would cut through the pelvis into upper and lower halves; the symphysis is a vertical midline structure.
The pubic symphysis is a midline structure, meaning it lies in the median sagittal plane, dividing the two hip bones anteriorly.
The transpyloric plane is at the level of the L1 vertebra, far superior to the pelvic girdle joints.
The coronal plane would separate the pelvis into front and back; the symphysis lies exactly in the middle of this front-to-back division.
The pelvic inlet lies in an oblique plane, but the articulation of the pubic symphysis itself is a strictly midline, sagittal orientation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The symphysis pubis... lies in the midline between the bodies of the pubic bones...

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: A 28-year-old female in the second stage of labor experiences a significant increase in the diameter of her pelvic outlet. Radiographic evidence suggests a temporary widening of the pelvic joints. Which joint is specifically designed to facilitate this change through hormone-induced loosening?
correctOption: Sacrococcygeal joint
optionExplanations: The sacrococcygeal joint is a symphysis that, under the influence of relaxin during pregnancy, loosens and allows the coccyx to be pushed posteriorly, increasing the anteroposterior diameter of the pelvic outlet.
The xiphisternal joint is in the thorax; its loosening would not assist in increasing the pelvic diameter for childbirth.
The TMJ is involved in mastication and is not affected by the pelvic-specific hormonal changes of parturition.
The atlanto-occipital joint is in the neck and does not participate in pelvic expansion.
While the lumbosacral joint allows flexion/extension, it is not one of the primary 'pelvic joints' (SI, PS, SC) described as loosening specifically for child passage in this context.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The pelvic joints are the sacroiliac joints, the pubic symphysis, and the sacrococcygeal joint. These normally strong joints may loosen somewhat to accommodate childbirth.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: The lumbosacral joint includes a disc between L5 and S1 and two zygapophysial joints. In the sagittal plane, what is the primary structural feature of the L5-S1 intervertebral disc that contributes to the formation of the lumbosacral angle?
options: The disc is significantly thicker anteriorly than posteriorly
The disc is thinner anteriorly to allow for lumbar kyphosis
The disc is circular in the horizontal plane and flat in the sagittal plane
The disc consists entirely of hyaline cartilage without a nucleus pulposus
The disc contains a high concentration of calcium hydroxyapatite
correctOption: The disc is significantly thicker anteriorly than posteriorly
optionExplanations: The lumbosacral angle (between the long axis of the lumbar column and the sacrum) is created largely because the L5-S1 intervertebral disc is wedge-shaped, being much thicker anteriorly. This supports the lumbar lordosis.
The lumbar spine exhibits lordosis (convexity anteriorly), requiring the disc to be thicker anteriorly. Kyphosis (convexity posteriorly) is not normal for the lumbar region.
The disc is wedge-shaped (not flat) in the sagittal plane; this wedging is essential for the transition from the mobile lumbar spine to the fixed sacrum.
All intervertebral discs (including L5-S1) possess an annulus fibrosus and a nucleus pulposus; they are not simple hyaline plates.
Calcium hydroxyapatite is found in bone; discs are fibrocartilaginous. Calcification of a disc is a pathological state (disc degeneration).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The posterior abdominal wall is formed in the midline by the five lumbar vertebrae and their intervertebral discs... The sacral promontory is the upper posterior margin of the pelvic inlet.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: Which of the following physiological changes occurs mechanically in the sacro-iliac and pubic symphysis joints to accommodate the passage of the fetus during labor?
options: Decreased distance between the ischial tuberosities
Loosening of the normally strong joint structures
Increased calcification of the joint capsules
correctOption: Loosening of the normally strong joint structures
optionExplanations: Ossification of the discs would fuse the joints, preventing the necessary expansion of the pelvic diameters required for birth.
The distance between ischial tuberosities should ideally increase or remain flexible; a decrease would narrow the pelvic outlet.
Ankylosis (fusion) of the sacrococcygeal joint would prevent the coccyx from being pushed posteriorly, potentially obstructing the birth canal.
Hormonal changes (such as relaxin) cause the ligaments and connective tissues of the pelvic joints to loosen, increasing the pelvic capacity.
Increased calcification would lead to joint rigidity, which is the opposite of the flexibility required for the pelvic outlet to expand during labor.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The pelvic joints are the sacroiliac joints, the pubic symphysis, and the sacrococcygeal joint. These normally strong joints may loosen somewhat to accommodate childbirth.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: The sacrococcygeal joint, which allows the coccyx to be pushed posteriorly during defecation or labor, is classified as which type of articulation?
correctOption: Symphysis
optionExplanations: The sacrococcygeal joint is a secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis) between the apex of the sacrum and the base of the coccyx, often containing a small intervertebral-like disc.
A gomphosis is a specialized fibrous 'peg-in-socket' joint found only between teeth and the alveolar bone of the jaws.
Sutures are fibrous joints restricted to the skull and do not allow the degree of movement seen in the sacrococcygeal junction.

Diarthrosis is a general term for synovial joints; while some sacrococcygeal joints may become synovial with age, it is typically classified as a symphysis in the context of pelvic mechanics during labor.
A synchondrosis is a primary cartilaginous joint that usually ossifies (like the epiphyseal plate), whereas the sacrococcygeal joint is a secondary cartilaginous joint with a fibrocartilaginous disc.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The pelvic joints are the sacroiliac joints, the pubic symphysis, and the sacrococcygeal joint. These normally strong joints may loosen somewhat to accommodate childbirth.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: Which anatomical structure provides the primary mechanical support to the pelvic joints by forming the greater and lesser sciatic foramina?
options: The transverse cervical and cardinal ligaments
correctOption: The sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments
optionExplanations: The inguinal and lacunar ligaments are associated with the anterior abdominal wall and the femoral canal, not the sciatic foramina.
The sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments anchor the sacrum to the hip bone (ischium), converting the sciatic notches into foramina and providing essential stability to the sacroiliac joint.
The round and broad ligaments are folds of peritoneum and vestiges of development that support the uterus, not the structural joints of the pelvis.
The transverse cervical (cardinal) ligaments are visceral pelvic fascia supporting the uterus and vagina.
The puboprostatic and pubovesical ligaments are thickenings of pelvic fascia that support the bladder and prostate, not the bony pelvis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments help form the greater and lesser sciatic foramina, which are parts of the pelvic outlet.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: Which joint serves as the articulation between the axial skeleton and the pelvic girdle?
correctOption: Sacro-iliac joint
optionExplanations: The shoulder joint connects the upper limb to the pectoral girdle, not the pelvic girdle.
Interphalangeal joints are distal appendicular joints within the digits.
The hip joint connects the pelvic girdle to the lower limb (femur), not the axial skeleton.
The sacro-iliac joint connects the sacrum (part of the axial skeleton) to the ilium (part of the pelvic girdle/appendicular skeleton).
The knee joint is an appendicular joint between the femur and tibia.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The bony pelvis consists of the paired hip bones (os coxae), the sacrum, and the coccyx.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: Anatomically, the sacroiliac joint is unique because it consists of two distinct types of articulations. Which surfaces constitute the synovial portion of this joint?
options: The sacral promontory and L5 body
The iliac crest and the transverse processes of S1
The auricular surfaces of the sacrum and ilium
The tuberosities of the sacrum and ilium
correctOption: The auricular surfaces of the sacrum and ilium
optionExplanations: The articulation between the sacral promontory and the L5 body is the lumbosacral joint (a symphysis), not part of the sacroiliac joint.
The iliac crest is a palpable landmark used to level S2, but it does not articulate with the S1 transverse processes to form a joint.
The anterior part of the sacroiliac joint is a synovial joint between the auricular (ear-shaped) surfaces of the sacrum and the ilium.
Ligaments support the joint but are not the articulating 'surfaces' that define the synovial cavity.
The tuberosities form the posterior syndesmotic portion of the joint, joined by strong interosseous ligaments, not the synovial part.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Each common iliac artery ends at the pelvic inlet in front of the sacroiliac joint by dividing into the external and internal iliac arteries.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: A clinician performs a digital rectal examination to assess the integrity of the pelvic floor and associated joints. Which bony part is palpable on the posterior aspect during this examination?
options: The anterior surface of the coccyx
correctOption: The anterior surface of the coccyx
optionExplanations: The pubic tubercle is an anterior landmark palpable via the scrotum or labia, not posteriorly via the rectum.
The internal urethral orifice is an anterior structure related to the bladder neck and prostate/vagina.
The coccyx lies immediately posterior to the anal canal and its anterior surface is easily felt by a gloved finger pointing posteriorly during a rectal exam.
The common iliac bifurcation occurs at the pelvic inlet (SIJ level), well above the reach of a standard digital rectal exam.
The iliac fossa is part of the lateral pelvic wall, too far lateral and superior for direct rectal palpation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The inferior surface and tip of the coccyx can be palpated in the cleft between the buttocks... The anterior surface of the coccyx can be palpated with the gloved finger in the anal canal.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: Which of the following joint types best classifies the pubic symphysis in the context of the adult bony pelvis?
correctOption: Secondary cartilaginous joint
optionExplanations: The pubic symphysis is a secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis), characterized by a fibrocartilaginous disc between the articular surfaces of the pubic bones, designed for weight-bearing and stability.
Fibrous syndesmoses involve interosseous ligaments, such as the posterior part of the sacroiliac joint, but the pubic symphysis uses fibrocartilage.
Primary cartilaginous joints (synchondroses) are joined by hyaline cartilage and typically ossify with age; the pubic symphysis remains cartilaginous throughout life.
Synovial joints are defined by a joint cavity and capsule; while the sacroiliac joint has a synovial component, the pubic symphysis does not.
Complex synovial joints involve multiple compartments or articular discs within a synovial capsule, which is not the morphology of the symphysis pubis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The pelvic joints are the sacroiliac joints, the pubic symphysis, and the sacrococcygeal joint. These normally strong joints may loosen somewhat to accommodate childbirth.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: During a pelvic surgery, a surgeon identifies a large venous vessel passing upward immediately anterior to the sacroiliac joint. Based on anatomical relations, which vessel is this most likely to be?
correctOption: Internal iliac vein
optionExplanations: The external iliac vein runs along the pelvic brim, medial to the psoas muscle, rather than directly in front of the sacroiliac joint.
The great saphenous vein is a superficial vein of the lower limb and does not enter the deep pelvic cavity near the sacroiliac joint.
The testicular vein runs on the posterior abdominal wall to the renal vein (left) or IVC (right), passing through the inguinal canal, not directly over the SI joint.
The inferior mesenteric vein is a tributary of the portal system and ascends on the posterior abdominal wall, far from the sacroiliac joint surface.
Correct. The internal iliac vein is specifically described as passing upward in front of the sacroiliac joint before joining the external iliac vein.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The internal iliac vein... passes upward in front of the sacroiliac joint and joins the external iliac vein to form the common iliac vein

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: The sacral promontory is an important obstetric landmark. It forms the anterior border of the superior articulation of which joint complex?
correctOption: Lumbosacral
optionExplanations: The pubic symphysis is the anterior-most joint of the pelvic ring.
The lumbosacral joint is the articulation between the fifth lumbar vertebra and the first sacral segment. The sacral promontory is the prominent anterior edge of the S1 vertebral body.
There is no 'ischiopubic joint'; the ischium and pubis fuse to form a single bone during puberty at the acetabulum.
The sacroiliac joints are lateral articulations between the auricular surfaces of the sacrum and the ilium.
The sacrococcygeal joint is at the inferior end of the sacrum, far from the promontory.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The sacral promontory is the upper posterior margin of the pelvic inlet and is an important obstetric landmark used when measuring the size of the pelvis.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: In the context of practical pelvic mechanics, why is the sacro-iliac joint's articulating surface irregular and pitted with elevations and depressions?
options: To provide interlocking stability for weight transmission
To facilitate the formation of the rectal ampulla
To increase surface area for the attachment of the common iliac artery
To permit high-velocity gliding during locomotion
To reduce the friction between the sacrum and the psoas muscle
correctOption: To provide interlocking stability for weight transmission
optionExplanations: The reciprocal irregularities (elevations and depressions) of the auricular surfaces provide an interlocking mechanism that, combined with strong ligaments, prevents the sacrum from slipping under the weight of the vertebral column.
The rectal ampulla is a soft tissue structure related to the pelvic floor; it does not depend on the SI joint's bony texture.
The common iliac artery lies *in front* of the joint but does not attach to its articulating surfaces.
High-velocity gliding is undesirable in the SI joint, which requires maximum stability to support the trunk's weight.
The psoas muscle lies on the lateral aspect of the lumbar vertebrae and pelvic brim, not between the articulating surfaces of the SI joint.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The common iliac artery ends at the pelvic inlet in front of the sacroiliac joint by dividing into the external and internal iliac arteries.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: Nutation and counter-nutation are the primary movements of the sacroiliac joint. Around which axis do these movements occur?
options: Transverse axis through the iliac tuberosities
Vertical axis through the pelvic inlet
Anteroposterior axis through the pubic symphysis
correctOption: Transverse axis through the iliac tuberosities
optionExplanations: The acetabulum is part of the hip joint, which has completely different mechanics and axes than the sacroiliac joint.
The sacrum rotates (tilts) around a transverse axis that passes through the interosseous sacroiliac ligaments/tuberosities. Nutation is the anterior tilt of the sacral base.
A vertical axis would allow rotation, which is extremely limited in the sacroiliac joint.
The femur is the articulating bone of the hip joint, not the sacroiliac joint.
An anteroposterior axis would allow lateral tilting (side-to-side), which the SI joint does not typically perform.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The posterior superior iliac spine... coincides with the level of the middle of the sacroiliac joint.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: At which specific location does the common iliac artery divide into its terminal branches in relation to the pelvic joints?
options: Directly superior to the symphysis pubis
Medial to the internal urethral orifice
correctOption: Anterior to the sacroiliac joint
optionExplanations: The symphysis pubis is the anterior-most point of the pelvis; the arteries are located more posteriorly near the sacroiliac articulation.
The ischial tuberosity is part of the pelvic outlet; the common iliac bifurcation is at the pelvic inlet.
The sacrococcygeal joint is the most inferior posterior joint; the common iliac bifurcation is at the pelvic inlet level.
The internal urethral orifice is located at the neck of the bladder, much more anterior and inferior than the common iliac bifurcation.
The bifurcation of the common iliac artery is a critical landmark occurring directly in front of the sacroiliac joint at the pelvic brim.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Each common iliac artery ends at the pelvic inlet in front of the sacroiliac joint by dividing into the external and internal iliac arteries.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: Which statement accurately describes the mechanics of movement and axes for the lumbosacral joint?
options: Movement is restricted to rotation around a vertical axis passing through the sacral canal.
It facilitates circumduction around a multi-axial ball and socket articulation.
It is a totally immobile fibrous synarthrosis designed for weight bearing only.
Movement is solely limited to lateral flexion in the coronal plane around an anterior-posterior axis.
Movement occurs primarily in the sagittal plane (flexion/extension) through the intervertebral disc and facet joints.
correctOption: Movement occurs primarily in the sagittal plane (flexion/extension) through the intervertebral disc and facet joints.
optionExplanations: Rotation at the L5-S1 level is very limited compared to the thoracic spine due to the orientation of the articular facets.
Only the hip and shoulder joints are ball-and-socket (spheroidal) joints in the human body; the lumbosacral joint is not.
The lumbosacral joint is a functional amphiarthrosis/diarthrosis combination; it is definitely not immobile.
Lateral flexion is possible but it is not the 'sole' or primary movement; flexion/extension is more pronounced.

The lumbosacral joint allows for significant flexion and extension (sagittal plane) as well as some lateral flexion. This occurs through the intervertebral disc and the posterior synovial facet joints.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The bony pelvis consists of the paired hip bones (os coxae), the sacrum, and the coccyx.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: A 45-year-old male presents with severe lower back pain and 'slippage' of the L5 vertebra over S1 visualized on a lateral radiograph. This clinical condition, spondylolisthesis, represents a failure of stability at which joint?
correctOption: Lumbosacral joint
optionExplanations: The sacrococcygeal joint is far distal to the L5-S1 junction.
Sacroiliac joint failure involves sacroiliitis or ligamentous rupture but not the sliding of a lumbar vertebra.

Spondylolisthesis specifically describes the anterior displacement of the L5 vertebral body over the S1 sacral base due to defects in the pars interarticularis or degenerative changes at the lumbosacral joint.
The sacrotuberous ligament is a stabilizing ligament of the sacroiliac joint/pelvic outlet, not a joint itself.
The pubic symphysis is an anterior joint; its failure results in diastasis, not vertebral slippage.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The bony pelvis consists of the paired hip bones (os coxae), the sacrum, and the coccyx. The pelvic brim divides the pelvis into an upper false pelvis and a lower true pelvis.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
coreConcept: Articulating Surfaces of the Sacrococcygeal Joint
statement: The sacrococcygeal joint is a symphysis between which specific anatomical parts?
options: The sacral hiatus and the perineal body
The sacral promontory and the pubic crest
Base of the sacrum and the L5 vertebral body
The auricular surface of the sacrum and the ilium
Apex of the sacrum and the base of the coccyx
correctOption: Apex of the sacrum and the base of the coccyx
optionExplanations: The sacral hiatus is an opening at the end of the sacral canal; the perineal body is a soft tissue mass in the perineum. They do not articulately unite.
The sacral promontory and pubic crest are parts of the pelvic brim (inlet) but do not articulate with each other.
This describes the lumbosacral joint, which is the junction between the spine and the pelvis.
This describes the articulating surfaces of the sacroiliac joint.
The sacrococcygeal joint is the articulation between the distal end (apex) of the sacrum and the proximal end (base) of the first coccygeal vertebra.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The pelvic joints are the sacroiliac joints, the pubic symphysis, and the sacrococcygeal joint.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: Where is the palpation point for the symphysis pubis located in a clinical surface examination?
options: At the level of the second sacral spine
In the midline between the bodies of the pubic bones
One inch behind the anus in the cleft
At the posterior end of the iliac crest
correctOption: In the midline between the bodies of the pubic bones
optionExplanations: The pubic tubercle is lateral to the pubic crest, which is lateral to the symphysis pubis itself.
The second sacral spine level marks the middle of the sacroiliac joint posteriorly, not the symphysis pubis anteriorly.
The symphysis pubis is the anterior midline articulation where the two pubic bones meet; it is palpable through the subcutaneous fat (mons pubis).
The tip of the coccyx, not the symphysis, is palpated one inch behind the anus in the gluteal cleft.
The posterior end of the iliac crest marks the posterior superior iliac spine, related to the sacroiliac joint.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The symphysis pubis... lies in the midline between the bodies of the pubic bones and can be palpated as a solid structure through the fat.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: What is the primary anatomical component that provides the structural union at the pubic symphysis?
correctOption: Fibrocartilaginous disc
optionExplanations: A secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis) is characterized by a central disc of fibrocartilage, which provides strength and shock absorption at the pubic symphysis.
Hyaline cartilage covers the articular surfaces but the primary union in a symphysis is fibrocartilage.
The joint is held by ligaments (superior and inferior pubic ligaments), but the structural union itself is fibrocartilaginous, not just a ligamentous sheet.
A synostosis is a complete bony fusion (like the adult hip bone); the pubic symphysis remains a cartilaginous union throughout life.
The pubic symphysis lacks a synovial cavity or membrane; it is a non-synovial joint.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The symphysis pubis... lies in the midline between the bodies of the pubic bones and can be palpated as a solid structure through the fat that is present in this region.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: A patient suffers a traumatic 'open book' pelvic fracture. The mechanical disruption involves the widening of the anterior pelvic midline and the stretching of the posterior pelvic ligaments. Which joints are primarily compromised in this scenario?
correctOption: Sacroiliac and Pubic Symphysis
optionExplanations: The sacrococcygeal and lumbosacral joints are not part of the primary pelvic ring that defines 'open book' fractures.
L4-L5 discs are superior to the bony pelvic ring and are involved in spinal rather than pelvic girdle integrity.
The acetabulofemoral joint is the hip; it is not typically part of the midline or posterior sacroiliac ring disruption defined here.
An 'open book' fracture refers to the disruption of the pubic symphysis (anteriorly) and the sacroiliac joints (posteriorly), breaking the 'pelvic ring'.
Disruption of the ischiopubic rami involves bone fracture, but the term 'open book' specifically implies joint diastasis of the symphysis and SI joint stress.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The pelvic joints are the sacroiliac joints, the pubic symphysis, and the sacrococcygeal joint.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: In the context of the bony pelvis, which landmark is defined as the upper posterior margin of the pelvic inlet?
correctOption: Sacral Promontory
optionExplanations: The sacral promontory is the specific bony projection of the S1 vertebra that marks the posterior boundary of the pelvic inlet.
The ischial spine is a landmark of the lateral pelvic wall and the pelvic outlet.
The anococcygeal body is a fibrous mass between the anus and coccyx, not a part of the inlet margin.
The pubic crest is part of the anterior margin of the pelvic inlet.
The sacral hiatus is the inferior opening of the sacral canal, located posteriorly near the coccyx.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The sacral promontory is the upper posterior margin of the pelvic inlet and is an important obstetric landmark used when measuring the size of the pelvis.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: A clinician performs a digital rectal exam to assess the posterior pelvic wall. Which joint's location is being assessed when palpating the cleft about 1 inch behind the anus?
correctOption: Sacrococcygeal joint
optionExplanations: Correct. The tip of the coccyx and the sacrococcygeal articulation are palpable in the midline cleft approximately 1 inch posterior to the anal orifice.
The lumbosacral joint is too superior to be palpated behind the anus.
The hip joint is a lateral articulation between the femur and the acetabulum, not a midline posterior structure.
The sacroiliac joints are deep and located higher and more laterally in the pelvic wall.
The pubic symphysis is an anterior joint and cannot be reached via the posterior cleft behind the anus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The inferior surface and tip of the coccyx can be palpated in the cleft between the buttocks about 1 in. (2.5 cm) behind the anus.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: During the third trimester of pregnancy, the physiological increase in relaxin levels alters the mechanics of the sacroiliac joints. What is the primary functional result of this change to facilitate childbirth?
options: Reduction of the pelvic inlet diameter
Increased range of nutation and counter-nutation
Rigid fixation of the sacral promontory
Permanent ossification of the sacroiliac ligaments
Conversion of the synovial joint into a synchondrosis
correctOption: Increased range of nutation and counter-nutation
optionExplanations: The mechanics are designed to increase pelvic diameters, not reduce them, to facilitate delivery.
Hormonal changes cause the sacroiliac ligaments to loosen, increasing the mechanics of nutation (sacral base moving anteriorly/inferiorly), which allows the pelvic outlet to expand during delivery.
Rigid fixation would prevent the necessary expansion of the pelvic diameters required for the passage of the fetal head.
Ossification would decrease mobility, which is the opposite of the physiological requirement for childbirth.
The joint does not change its basic structural type (synovial/syndesmosis mix); only the laxity of the supporting connective tissue is altered.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": These normally strong joints may loosen somewhat to accommodate childbirth.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: During the movement of counternutation at the sacroiliac joint, what is the mechanical effect on the pelvic diameters?
options: The pelvic inlet increases while the pelvic outlet decreases.
Both inlet and outlet diameters decrease simultaneously.
The pelvic inlet decreases while the pelvic outlet increases.
Both inlet and outlet diameters increase simultaneously.
The transverse diameter increases while the sagittal diameter remains fixed.
correctOption: The pelvic inlet increases while the pelvic outlet decreases.
optionExplanations: Counternutation involves the posterior and superior movement of the sacral promontory. This increases the anteroposterior diameter of the pelvic inlet but simultaneously moves the coccyx forward, decreasing the outlet diameter.
Pelvic joints are designed to allow compensatory expansion; a reduction in both would be pathological rather than physiological.
This describes nutation, where the sacral promontory moves anteriorly (decreasing inlet) and the coccyx moves posteriorly (increasing outlet).
The sacrum acts as a lever; movements that increase one opening of the true pelvis typically reduce the other in the sagittal plane.
The primary movements of the sacrum are in the sagittal plane (AP diameter changes), not the transverse plane, which is limited by the strong sacroiliac ligaments/hip bones.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The pelvic joints are the sacroiliac joints, the pubic symphysis, and the sacrococcygeal joint. These normally strong joints may loosen somewhat to accommodate childbirth.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: Which specific bony features articulate to form the sacro-iliac joint, and how do they differ in their structural classification across the joint surface?
options: The sacral hiatus and the iliac fossa; purely cartilaginous
The median sacral crest and the iliac spine; purely fibrous
The ischial tuberosity and the coccyx; purely synovial
The auricular surfaces; synovial anteriorly and syndesmosis posteriorly
The sacral promontory and the pubic crest; purely fibrous
correctOption: The auricular surfaces; synovial anteriorly and syndesmosis posteriorly
optionExplanations: The sacral hiatus is an opening at the lower end of the sacral canal and does not participate in joint articulation.
The median sacral crest is formed by fused spinous processes and does not articulate with the ilium.
The ischial tuberosity does not articulate with the coccyx; it serves as an attachment point for the sacrotuberous ligament.
The sacro-iliac joint is unique: the anterior portion is a synovial joint between auricular surfaces, while the posterior part is a fibrous syndesmosis.
The sacral promontory is a landmark for the inlet, not the primary articular surface of the sacro-iliac joint.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The pelvic joints are the sacroiliac joints, the pubic symphysis, and the sacrococcygeal joint.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
coreConcept: Arterial landmarks of the pelvic inlet
statement: The common iliac artery bifurcation, a key surgical landmark, occurs in which anatomical plane relative to the pelvic joints?
options: Directly inferior to the inguinal ligament
In front of the sacro-iliac joint
correctOption: In front of the sacro-iliac joint
optionExplanations: The pubic symphysis is the anterior-most midline landmark, while the arterial bifurcation is posterior and lateral.
At the inguinal ligament, the external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery; this is distal to the bifurcation.
The sacrococcygeal joint is the most inferior part of the sacrum; the bifurcation occurs at the superior pelvic inlet level.
The ischial tuberosity is part of the pelvic outlet (inferior), whereas the bifurcation is at the pelvic inlet (superior).
The common iliac artery reaches the pelvic inlet and divides into internal and external branches specifically in the space immediately anterior to the sacro-iliac joint.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Each common iliac artery ends at the pelvic inlet in front of the sacroiliac joint by dividing into the external and internal iliac arteries

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: The lumbosacral joint is a complex articulation consisting of a symphysis and two synovial joints. Which structures specifically articulate at the synovial portion of this joint?
options: The lamina of L5 and the median sacral crest
The body of L5 and the sacral promontory
The pedicles of L5 and the lateral mass of the sacrum
The transverse processes of L5 and the ala of the sacrum
The inferior articular processes of L5 and the superior articular processes of S1
correctOption: The inferior articular processes of L5 and the superior articular processes of S1
optionExplanations: The lamina and the median sacral crest are sites of ligamentous attachment (ligamentum flavum/interspinous ligaments) and do not articulate directly.
The articulation between the body of L5 and the sacral promontory is a secondary cartilaginous joint involving an intervertebral disc, not a synovial joint.
Pedicles form the sides of the vertebral arch and do not have articular surfaces for synovial joints; the lateral mass of the sacrum articulates with the ilium at the sacroiliac joint.
The transverse processes of L5 are connected to the ilium and sacrum by the strong iliolumbar and lumbosacral ligaments, but they do not form a synovial articulation.

The synovial portion of the lumbosacral joint consists of the right and left zygapophysial joints (facet joints) between the inferior articular processes of the L5 vertebra and the superior articular processes of the S1 vertebra.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The posterior abdominal wall is formed in the midline by the five lumbar vertebrae and their intervertebral discs and laterally by... the upper part of the bony pelvis.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
coreConcept: Vulnerability of Viscera to Pelvic Fracture
statement: A 24-year-old male presents following a high-velocity motor vehicle accident with a crushed pelvis. Radiographs show a 4cm separation at the pubic symphysis (diastasis). Based on the anatomic relations of the bladder in the presence of such pelvic fractures, where is the most likely site of bladder injury?
options: Intraperitoneal rupture of the superior wall
Compression of the ureter at the sacroiliac joint
Extraperitoneal rupture of the anterior wall
Rupture of the urachus at the umbilicus
Avulsion of the internal urethral sphincter from the prostate
correctOption: Extraperitoneal rupture of the anterior wall
optionExplanations: Intraperitoneal rupture usually occurs when a full bladder is subjected to blunt force, not typically as a result of piercing bony fragments from a fracture.
While the ureter crosses the SIJ, it is less commonly ruptured by symphysis diastasis compared to the anterior bladder wall.
The anterior bladder wall lies immediately behind the pubic bones; pelvic fractures often result in bony shards piercing this extraperitoneal area.
The urachus (median umbilical ligament) is a fibrous remnant; its rupture is rare and unrelated to pelvic joint diastasis.
While the bladder neck rests on the prostate, direct anterior wall piercing by pubic fragments is the classic complication of symphysis rupture.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Extraperitoneal rupture involves the anterior part of the bladder wall below the level of the peritoneal reflection. It most commonly occurs in fractures of the pelvis when bony fragments pierce the bladder wall.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: The sacrococcygeal joint, which allows the coccyx to be pushed posteriorly during defecation or labor, is characterized as which type of articulation?
correctOption: Secondary cartilaginous joint
optionExplanations: Primary cartilaginous joints are temporary and lack a fibrocartilaginous disc, whereas this joint persists with a disc into adulthood.
The sacrococcygeal joint is a secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis), containing a fibrocartilaginous disc that permits significant passive mobility.
A synovial hinge joint (like the elbow) has a cavity and allows flexion/extension; the sacrococcygeal joint is united by a disc.
Syndesmosis joints are united by interosseous ligaments (like the distal tibiofibular joint), not a fibrocartilaginous disc.
Sutural joints are found exclusively between the bones of the skull, not in the vertebral column or pelvis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The pelvic joints are the sacroiliac joints, the pubic symphysis, and the sacrococcygeal joint.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: Which artery is specifically noted to divide into its external and internal branches immediately anterior to the sacroiliac joint?
correctOption: Common iliac artery
optionExplanations: The superior rectal artery is a terminal branch of the inferior mesenteric artery and descends into the pelvis, but it is not the vessel that divides into internal/external iliacs.
The common iliac artery travels down to the pelvic brim and bifurcates into the internal and external iliac arteries directly anterior to the sacroiliac joint.
The median sacral artery is a small midline vessel arising from the aortic bifurcation and descending over the sacrum, it does not divide at the SI joint.
The abdominal aorta bifurcates into the common iliac arteries at the L4 level, which is superior to the sacroiliac joint.
The inferior mesenteric artery arises from the aorta and continues as the superior rectal artery; it does not bifurcate at the SI joint.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Each common iliac artery ends at the pelvic inlet in front of the sacroiliac joint by dividing into the external and internal iliac arteries.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: Which of the following bones participate in the formation of the pubic symphysis joint?
options: Acetabular margin and the pubic tubercle
Ischial tuberosity and the inferior ramus of the pubis
Superior ramus of the pubis and the iliac crest
Bodies of the pubic bones in the midline
Body of the ilium and the pubic crest
correctOption: Bodies of the pubic bones in the midline
optionExplanations: The acetabular margin is the rim of the hip socket for the femur, unrelated to the anterior midline symphysis joint.
The ischial tuberosity is a posterior-inferior feature used for weight bearing while sitting, not for the pubic symphysis.
The iliac crest is the superior border of the ilium; it does not articulate with the pubic bones in the midline.
The pubic symphysis is a secondary cartilaginous joint formed by the union of the bodies of the two pubic bones in the median plane.
The body of the ilium forms the superior part of the hip bone and acetabulum, not the pubic symphysis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The symphysis pubis (see Figs. 8.1 and 8.22) lies in the midline between the bodies of the pubic bones and can be palpated as a solid structure through the fat that is present in this region.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: Which of the following constitutes the trio of articulations specifically classified as the 'pelvic joints' in clinical anatomy?
correctOption: Sacroiliac, Pubic Symphysis, and Sacrococcygeal
optionExplanations: The sacroiliac joints, pubic symphysis, and sacrococcygeal joint are the three articulations that form the semi-rigid pelvic ring and respond to pregnancy hormones.
The iliopectineal and ischiopubic lines/rami are parts of the hip bone but do not represent the primary mobile joints of the pelvis.
The acetabular 'joint' (triradiate cartilage) is a site of fusion within the hip bone, not a joint of the pelvic girdle as a whole.
The 'obturator' is not a joint; it is a foramen covered by a membrane.
The iliofemoral joint is the hip joint and is not considered a primary 'pelvic joint' in the context of the pelvic girdle's internal articulations.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The pelvic joints are the sacroiliac joints, the pubic symphysis, and the sacrococcygeal joint.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: During the final stages of pregnancy and labor, what physiological mechanism occurs in the sacroiliac and pubic joints to facilitate the passage of the fetal head through the birth canal?
options: Hormone-induced loosening of the strong ligaments
Decrease in the anorectal angle by puborectalis contraction
Synovial fluid reduction to increase friction
Rigid fixation of the sacral promontory
correctOption: Hormone-induced loosening of the strong ligaments
optionExplanations: Ossification would make the joints more rigid and smaller, which would obstruct labor rather than assist it.
Under the influence of hormones like relaxin, the ligaments of the sacroiliac joints and pubic symphysis loosen, allowing the pelvic diameters to increase slightly during parturition.
While the puborectalis muscle relates to the pelvic floor, its relaxation (not contraction) is required for defecation/labor, and it does not describe the mechanic of the joints themselves.
A reduction in synovial fluid would decrease joint mobility; labor requires increased pelvic capacity through joint expansion.
Rigid fixation of the sacral promontory would prevent the nutation required to enlarge the pelvic outlet.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": These normally strong joints may loosen somewhat to accommodate childbirth.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: The sacral promontory, a key feature of the lumbosacral region, serves what primary function in obstetric practice?
options: As a site for the insertion of the internal urethral sphincter
To act as the pivot point for the puborectalis muscle sling
To mark the termination of the extra-dural space
As a landmark for measuring the capacity of the pelvic inlet
To provide attachment for the levator ani muscles
correctOption: As a landmark for measuring the capacity of the pelvic inlet
optionExplanations: The internal urethral sphincter is located at the neck of the bladder, which is related to the symphysis pubis, not the sacral promontory.
The puborectalis sling attaches to the pubic bones anteriorly and loops around the anorectal junction, not the sacral promontory.
The extra-dural space terminates at the sacral hiatus, which is at the distal end of the sacrum, not the proximal promontory.
Obstetricians use the sacral promontory to calculate the conjugate diameters of the pelvic inlet to ensure the head can engage.
The levator ani originates from the pubic bone and the tendinous arch of the pelvic fascia, not the sacral promontory.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The sacral promontory is the upper posterior margin of the pelvic inlet and is an important obstetric landmark used when measuring the size of the pelvis.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: During a physical examination, a clinician uses the posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) as a landmark for joint localization. Which joint's middle portion corresponds to the level of the PSIS?
correctOption: Sacroiliac joint
optionExplanations: Correct. The PSIS is the clinical landmark for the second sacral spine level and specifically marks the middle of the sacroiliac joint articulation.
The sacrococcygeal joint is located much lower, approximately 2 inches below the sacral hiatus, near the tip of the coccyx.
The hip joint is located laterally and inferiorly to the PSIS; the greater trochanter is its more relevant surface landmark.
The lumbosacral joint is located at a higher vertebral level than the PSIS, which is at the level of the second sacral spine.
The pubic symphysis is an anterior structure, whereas the PSIS is a posterior landmark.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": It [Posterior superior iliac spine] also coincides with the level of the middle of the sacroiliac joint.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: In the context of pelvic mechanics, how does the internal iliac vein relate to the sacro-iliac joint as it forms the common iliac vein?
options: It lies medial to the pubic symphysis
It passes upward in front of the sacro-iliac joint
It runs inferior to the sacrococcygeal joint
It passes posterior to the sacro-iliac joint
correctOption: It passes upward in front of the sacro-iliac joint
optionExplanations: The internal iliac vein is deep in the posterior pelvis, whereas the pubic symphysis is the most anterior midline structure.
The vein does not pierce the joint; it travels within the extraperitoneal space anterior to the joint capsule.
The internal iliac vein ascends on the anterior aspect of the sacro-iliac joint before merging with the external iliac vein.
The sacrococcygeal joint is far more inferior and midline than the course of the internal iliac vein.
The vein is situated anterior (in front) to the joint, not posterior to the bony articulation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The internal iliac vein... passes upward in front of the sacroiliac joint and joins the external iliac vein to form the common iliac vein.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: The lumbosacral joint is reinforced by strong ligaments to prevent the L5 vertebra from sliding anteriorly over the sacrum. What specific landmark on the sacrum articulates with the L5 intervertebral disc?
correctOption: Sacral promontory
optionExplanations: The sacral canal is the central tunnel for nerve roots; while L5 nerves pass near it, the canal itself is not the articular surface for the disc.
The apex of the sacrum is the inferior end that articulates with the coccyx, not the L5 vertebra.
The median sacral crest represents fused spinous processes on the posterior surface; it does not articulate with the L5 disc.
The sacral promontory is the anterior-superior edge of the S1 vertebral body, which articualtes with the L5-S1 intervertebral disc at the lumbosacral joint.
The sacral hiatus is an opening at the inferior end of the sacral canal, used for caudal anesthesia, not an articulation site for L5.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The sacral promontory is the upper posterior margin of the pelvic inlet and is an important obstetric landmark...

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: A 35-year-old female in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with sharp, localized pain over the anterior pelvic midline that radiates to the groins, exacerbated by walking and weight-bearing on one leg. Physical examination reveals exquisite tenderness over the symphysis pubis. Which physiologic changes in the mechanics of the pelvic joints best explain this differential diagnosis?
options: Calcification of the iliolumbar ligaments limiting L5 movement
Decreased production of synovial fluid in the sacroiliac joint
Increased laxity of the interpubic ligaments and widening of the joint space due to Relaxin
Anterior tilting of the coccyx reducing the pelvic outlet
Premature ossification of the triradiate cartilage in the acetabulum
correctOption: Increased laxity of the interpubic ligaments and widening of the joint space due to Relaxin
optionExplanations: Calcification would decrease mobility; the pain in pregnancy arises from hypermobility and ligamentous stretching.
Pregnancy actually increases pelvic joint mobility; a decrease in synovial fluid (typical of osteoarthritis) is not the mechanism for acute pregnancy-related symphyseal pain.

Symphysis Pubis Dysfunction (SPD) is common in pregnancy. The hormone relaxin increases the laxity of the fibrocartilage and supporting ligaments (superior and inferior pubic) to prepare for birth, often leading to painful instability and widening of the symphyseal cleft.
The coccyx moves posteriorly (counternutation) during the second stage of labor to *increase* the outlet; anterior tilting would decrease it and is not the primary cause of midline pubic pain.
Triradiate cartilage fuses during puberty (late teens); it is not involved in pregnancy-related pelvic pain.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The pelvic joints are the sacroiliac joints, the pubic symphysis, and the sacrococcygeal joint. These normally strong joints may loosen somewhat to accommodate childbirth.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: Regarding the mechanics of movement at the sacroiliac joint, what is the term used to describe the forward tilting of the sacral promontory while the coccyx moves posteriorly?
correctOption: Nutation
optionExplanations: Nutation (from Latin 'nodding') occurs when the sacral base/promontory tilts anteriorly and inferiorly. This movement is limited by strong ligaments but increases during labor.
Inversion is a movement of the foot/ankle complex, not used to describe sacroiliac joint mechanics.
Counter-nutation is the opposite movement, where the sacral promontory moves posteriorly and the sacral apex moves anteriorly.
Anteversion refers to the forward tilting of the entire uterus relative to the vagina, not a movement of the sacroiliac joint.
Anteflexion refers to the forward bending of the body of the uterus on the cervix, not a joint mechanic.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The pelvic joints are the sacroiliac joints, the pubic symphysis, and the sacrococcygeal joint. These normally strong joints may loosen somewhat to accommodate childbirth.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: The sacroiliac joint is characterized anatomically as a combination of two distinct types of articulations. Which of the following accurately describes the classification of this joint as it relates to its anterior and posterior components?
options: Anterior gomphosis and posterior synovial joint
Anterior synovial joint and posterior syndesmosis
Anterior syndesmosis and posterior synovial joint
correctOption: Anterior synovial joint and posterior syndesmosis
optionExplanations: A symphysis is found in the midline of the pelvis (pubic symphysis), but the sacroiliac joint does not utilize a fibrocartilaginous disc for its primary articulation.
Gomphoses are specific fibrous joints (peg-in-socket) found only in the alveolar processes of the jaws for teeth; they are not found in the pelvis.

The sacroiliac joint is unique; its anterior surface between the auricular surfaces of the sacrum and ilium is a synovial joint, while the posterior portion is a fibrous syndesmosis where the tuberosities are joined by interosseous ligaments.

Synchondroses are primary cartilaginous joints involving hyaline cartilage, while symphyses are secondary cartilaginous joints; these do not define the specific anterior/posterior split of the sacroiliac joint.
This is the reverse of the actual anatomy; the synovial cavity is located anteriorly, while the syndesmotic fibrous connection is located posteriorly to provide maximum weight-bearing stability.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The pelvic joints are the sacroiliac joints, the pubic symphysis, and the sacrococcygeal joint. These normally strong joints may loosen somewhat to accommodate childbirth.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: Which specific structure provides the articulating surface for the pubic symphysis in the midline of the pelvis?
correctOption: Body of the pubic bone
optionExplanations: The ischial tuberosity is the postero-inferior weight-bearing part of the hip bone; it is not a joint surface for the symphysis.
The iliac crest is the superior border of the ilium, serving as a muscle attachment site, not an articulation point.
The pubic symphysis is the midline articulation between the medial surfaces of the bodies of the right and left pubic bones.
The inferior pubic ramus joins the ischial ramus to form the ischiopubic ramus, which bounds the obturator foramen, but the symphysis occurs at the pubic body.
The acetabular labrum is a fibrocartilaginous rim around the hip joint socket, not involved in the midline symphysis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The symphysis pubis... lies in the midline between the bodies of the pubic bones.

category: Describe the type, articulations and mechanics of movements {axes and planes} of the following joints: 1) Sacro-Iliac 2) Pubic Symphysis 3) Lumbosacral 4) Sacrococcygeal
statement: Which of the following describes the anatomical position of the empty urinary bladder relative to the pubic symphysis in an adult?
correctOption: Immediately posterior
optionExplanations: The bladder is a midline structure and is not lateral to the pubic crest.
The bladder only rises superior to the symphysis into the abdominal cavity when it is full.
No major pelvic viscera lie anterior to the pubic symphysis; only subcutaneous tissue, fat, and skin are anterior.
The bladder is superior to the urogenital diaphragm; the neck of the female bladder rests on its upper surface.
The pubic symphysis provides a protective anterior shield for the bladder; thus, the empty bladder resides in the retropubic space immediately posterior to it.
